questionText: Listen to a conversation at the student center about signing up for a career skills workshop.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits the student center front desk to register for a career skills workshop on resume writing.
Tyler: Hi, I saw a flyer about a resume writing workshop next week. Can I still sign up?
Coordinator: Absolutely. The workshop is next Wednesday at two PM in Room 214. There are still seats available. May I have your name and student ID?
Tyler: Tyler Marsh, ID eight-four-nine-two-zero-seven.
Coordinator: Great, you're registered. Please bring a printed copy of your current resume and a job description for a position you're interested in. The facilitator will use those for the hands-on revision segment.
Tyler: I don't have a job description yet. Is that a problem?
Coordinator: Not at all. If you don't have one, the facilitator will provide sample postings. But bringing your own makes the exercises more tailored to your goals.
Tyler: That makes sense. Is there a fee?
Coordinator: The workshop is free for all enrolled students. However, if you register and don't show up without canceling twenty-four hours in advance, a ten-dollar no-show fee will be charged to your account. That policy helps us manage waitlisted students.
Tyler: Understood. How long is the workshop?
Coordinator: It runs for ninety minutes, from two to three thirty PM. There's also an optional fifteen-minute Q&A at the end if you want to stay and ask the facilitator specific questions.
Tyler: Perfect. Can I bring a friend who isn't registered?
Coordinator: Walk-ins are welcome if seats remain, but registered students get priority. I'd recommend your friend sign up online tonight to guarantee a spot.
Tyler: I'll let him know. Thanks for your help.
Coordinator: You're welcome. You'll get a confirmation email with the room details and a reminder the day before.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the academic office about preparing for a study abroad program.
audioScript:
Situation: A student meets with a study abroad advisor to prepare documents and deadlines for a semester in Spain.
Advisor: Come in, Sofia. You mentioned you're planning to study in Madrid next spring. Let's go over what you need.
Sofia: Yes, I'm really excited but a bit overwhelmed. I know I need a passport, but I'm not sure what else.
Advisor: First, check your passport expiration. Spain requires it to be valid for at least six months beyond your return date. If yours expires soon, renew it now because processing takes eight to ten weeks.
Sofia: Mine expires in March of next year, and I return in December. So that's only three months. I'll need to renew it.
Advisor: Correct. Next, you'll need a student visa. The Spanish consulate requires a letter of acceptance from your host university, proof of financial support, and a background check. The background check must be apostilled, which adds about four weeks.
Sofia: Four weeks just for the apostille? When is the visa application deadline?
Advisor: The consulate recommends submitting your visa application at least sixty days before departure. You're leaving January fifteenth, so aim to have everything ready by mid-November.
Sofia: That's tight. I don't have the acceptance letter yet.
Advisor: The host university sends it electronically within two weeks of your program approval. Your program was approved last Friday, so you should receive it by this Friday.
Sofia: Oh good. What about the financial support proof?
Advisor: You can use a bank statement showing sufficient funds, or a notarized letter from a sponsor, typically a parent, confirming they'll cover your expenses. The minimum amount is six thousand euros for one semester.
Sofia: My parents said they'd sponsor me. I'll ask them for the notarized letter. Are there any scholarships I can apply for?
Advisor: Yes, the Global Education Fund offers grants up to three thousand dollars. The application requires two faculty recommendations and a five-hundred-word essay. The deadline is October first.
Sofia: That's coming up. I'll start the essay this week.
Advisor: Good plan. I'll email you a checklist of all documents and deadlines so nothing slips through the cracks.

questionText: Listen to a conversation at the housing office about submitting a campus housing application.
audioScript:
Situation: A sophomore student speaks with a housing office clerk about applying for on-campus housing for the next academic year.
Marcus: Hi, I'd like to apply for on-campus housing for next year. I'm a sophomore now, and I want to know if I'm guaranteed a spot.
Clerk: Unfortunately, on-campus housing is only guaranteed for freshmen. Sophomores and above enter a lottery system. You'll need to submit your application by March fifteenth to be included.
Marcus: A lottery? What are my chances?
Clerk: Last year, about seventy percent of sophomores who applied received a housing offer. It depends on how many students apply and how many beds are available. Priority is given to students with documented medical accommodations.
Marcus: I don't have a medical accommodation, but I do have a work-study job on campus. Does that help?
Clerk: Work-study status doesn't affect housing priority directly. However, there is a limited number of rooms reserved for resident advisors. If you're interested in becoming an RA, the application opens in January and includes free housing as a benefit.
Marcus: That's interesting. What does the RA role involve?
Clerk: RAs are responsible for about forty residents on their floor. Duties include organizing events, enforcing policies, mediating conflicts, and being on call one weeknight per week and one weekend per month. It's a significant time commitment, but the free housing and a meal plan are included.
Marcus: That sounds like a lot. If I just go with the lottery, when would I find out?
Clerk: Lottery results are emailed by April tenth. If you get a spot, you'll have one week to accept and pay a three-hundred-dollar housing deposit. If you don't get a spot, you'll be placed on a waitlist and notified if openings come up over the summer.
Marcus: Can I choose my roommate either way?
Clerk: Yes, both lottery winners and waitlisted students can request a specific roommate, as long as that person also lists you. Roommate requests must be mutual to be honored.
Marcus: Got it. I'll submit my application this week and think about the RA option.
Clerk: Sounds good. The application is available on the housing portal. Let me know if you have any questions.

questions.explanation: The clerk explains that on-campus housing is only guaranteed for freshmen, and sophomores and above enter a lottery system.

questionText: Listen to a conversation at the campus cafeteria about joining the student magazine staff.
audioScript:
Situation: Two students talk at the cafeteria about one student's interest in joining the campus magazine as a staff writer.
Emma: Hey Jared, I heard you're thinking about joining The Campus Voice. I've been on the staff since last fall.
Jared: Yeah, I love writing and thought it'd be a good way to get involved. What's the process to join?
Emma: First, you submit two writing samples, ideally one news article and one opinion piece, through our online portal. The editorial board reviews them and schedules an interview if they're interested.
Jared: What are they looking for in the samples?
Emma: They want to see clear structure, engaging voice, and factual accuracy. For the news piece, make sure you cite at least two sources. For the opinion piece, they value a strong, well-supported argument rather than just a rant.
Jared: I have a news article I wrote for my journalism class last semester. Would that work?
Emma: Definitely, class assignments are fine. As long as it hasn't been published elsewhere. We want original content. Once you're on staff, you're expected to write at least one article per issue, and we publish biweekly.
Jared: One article every two weeks seems manageable. Are there editorial meetings I'd need to attend?
Emma: Yes, we have pitch meetings every other Tuesday at six PM in the media lab. Everyone brings two or three story ideas and the team votes on which ones to assign. Attendance is mandatory unless you have a class conflict.
Jared: What if I can't make a Tuesday meeting because of a lab?
Emma: You can submit your pitches by email beforehand, but you should try to attend at least seventy-five percent of meetings per semester or you could be removed from staff.
Jared: That's fair. Is the position paid?
Emma: Staff writers are unpaid, but editors receive a small stipend of two hundred dollars per semester. After one semester on staff, you can apply for an editor position. There are section editors for news, features, opinion, and arts.
Jared: I'd love to aim for opinion editor eventually. I'll submit my samples this week.
Emma: Great! The deadline for this round is Friday. Let me know if you need feedback before you submit.

questionText: Listen to a conversation on campus between two students about running for student government.
audioScript:
Situation: Two students discuss the process and rules for running for student government positions on the campus quad.
Nina: Ravi, I saw your campaign posters. You're running for student body president? That's awesome!
Ravi: Thanks! I decided to run because I want to push for extended library hours and more funding for student clubs. But honestly, the election rules are confusing. I've been reading the election code all morning.
Nina: I was on the election committee last year. Maybe I can help. What's confusing you?
Ravi: First, how many signatures do I need on my nomination petition?
Nina: For president, you need two hundred signatures from currently enrolled students. For vice president, it's one hundred fifty. Make sure each signer includes their student ID number, or the signature won't count.
Ravi: Two hundred? I only have about a hundred and twenty so far. The deadline is this Friday. What happens if I don't get enough?
Nina: Then your name won't appear on the ballot. But you can still run as a write-in candidate. Write-in votes are counted, but it's much harder to win that way since your name isn't printed on the ballot.
Ravi: I'd rather get the signatures. Are there spending limits on campaigning?
Nina: Yes, each presidential ticket can spend up to three hundred dollars total. You have to submit receipts to the election committee within forty-eight hours of the polls closing. Going over the limit results in disqualification.
Ravi: Three hundred is tight. Does that include the cost of printing posters?
Nina: Yes, everything counts, posters, buttons, flyers, even food you give away at campaign events. The only exception is digital posts on official university platforms, which are free.
Ravi: Good to know. When is the actual election?
Nina: Voting opens online on Monday at eight AM and closes Wednesday at eight PM. Results are announced Thursday evening at the election rally in the student center.
Ravi: And how do students vote?
Nina: They log in to the student portal with their ID and select their candidates. Each student gets one vote for president and one for vice president. It's all electronic now, no paper ballots.
Ravi: Thanks, Nina. This clears up a lot. I'll focus on getting those signatures by Friday.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the library between two students about preparing for a debate tournament.
audioScript:
Situation: Two members of the debate team meet in the library to prepare arguments for an upcoming intercollegiate tournament.
Grace: Okay Sam, the tournament is in two weeks and our resolution is about whether the government should implement a universal basic income. I'll take the affirmative and you'll take the negative. Let's compare our research.
Sam: Sounds good. I've gathered three main arguments against UBI. First, the cost is prohibitive. Studies show a nationwide UBI in the US would cost over three trillion dollars annually, requiring massive tax increases.
Grace: That's a strong point. On the affirmative side, I have evidence from the Finland UBI experiment showing that recipients reported lower stress and better mental health without reducing employment rates.
Sam: I actually have a counter to that. The Finland experiment was small-scale, only two thousand participants, and lasted just two years. Critics argue it can't be generalized to a national population.
Grace: That's fair, but I can cite the Alaska Permanent Fund, which has distributed dividends to all residents since 1982. That's a longer-term example, though the amount is much smaller than a full UBI.
Sam: Good, I'll need to address that. My second argument is about work disincentives. A study from the University of Chicago found that a twelve-thousand-dollar annual UBI could reduce employment by five percent nationally.
Grace: I have a rebuttal for that. The same study noted the reduction was concentrated among secondary earners, not primary breadwinners, meaning overall household income remained stable. Also, other studies show UBI can actually encourage entrepreneurship by providing a safety net.
Sam: I'll need to find evidence questioning that entrepreneurship claim. What's your second affirmative argument?
Grace: My second pillar is that UBI simplifies the welfare system by replacing multiple overlapping programs, reducing administrative costs and bureaucratic inefficiency.
Sam: That's interesting but risky. Some economists argue that targeted programs are more efficient because they direct resources to those who need them most, rather than giving money to everyone including the wealthy.
Grace: That's where we'll clash. I think the simplicity argument resonates with judges who value administrative efficiency. What's your third argument?
Sam: My third is inflation risk. Injecting that much purchasing power into the economy could drive up prices, especially in housing, effectively canceling out the benefit.
Grace: That's compelling. I need to find evidence on whether UBI is inflationary or not. Let's split the remaining research: I'll look for inflation counter-evidence, and you find studies supporting your entrepreneurship skepticism.
Sam: Deal. We should also practice cross-examination. The tournament format gives each side three minutes of cross-ex. I tend to ask too many leading questions, so I need to work on open-ended ones.
Grace: Same here. Let's schedule a mock debate for next Thursday in the speech room. We'll each give our full constructive speeches and do cross-ex.
Sam: Perfect. I'll book the room. Let's reconvene on Monday to share what we find.

questionText: Listen to a conversation in the academic office between a student and a professor about a peer review session.
audioScript:
Situation: A student visits a professor during office hours to discuss feedback received during a peer review session for a research paper.
Professor Lin: Come in, Derek. You said you wanted to talk about the peer review feedback on your draft. What's on your mind?
Derek: Thanks, Professor Lin. I'm a bit confused because my two peer reviewers gave me contradictory feedback. One said my thesis was too narrow, and the other said it was too broad. I'm not sure how to revise.
Professor Lin: That's actually common in peer review. Let's look at your thesis together. Read it for me?
Derek: It says, 'Social media algorithms reinforce political polarization by prioritizing engaging content over diverse viewpoints.'
Professor Lin: I see the issue. The thesis is specific about the mechanism, algorithms prioritizing engagement, but it's broad in scope because 'social media' covers many platforms. One reviewer likely felt the mechanism was clear while the scope was unmanageable for a ten-page paper.
Derek: So how do I fix it?
Professor Lin: Narrow the scope to one or two platforms. For example, 'Twitter's algorithm reinforces political polarization by prioritizing engaging content over diverse viewpoints.' That keeps your mechanism but makes the paper feasible within the page limit.
Derek: That makes sense. One reviewer also said my methodology section lacked detail on how I measured polarization. What should I add?
Professor Lin: You need to define your measurement framework. Are you using survey data, content analysis, or a polarization index? For a paper of this length, I'd recommend citing an established index, like the Esteban-Ray polarization measure, and explaining how you apply it to your dataset.
Derek: I was planning to use survey data from the Pew Research Center. Would that work with the Esteban-Ray measure?
Professor Lin: It can, but you'd need to explain how you convert survey responses into the ideological distance scores the formula requires. That conversion step is what your reviewer was missing. Add a subsection, maybe half a page, on data transformation.
Derek: Got it. The second reviewer said my conclusion was too abrupt. Any advice?
Professor Lin: A good conclusion should restate your thesis in light of the evidence, acknowledge limitations, and suggest future research. Right now yours just summarizes findings. Add a paragraph on limitations, such as the fact that your study covers only one platform, and another paragraph on future directions, like extending the analysis to multiple platforms.
Derek: That's helpful. When is the final paper due?
Professor Lin: The final draft is due in two weeks, on the twenty-third. I'd recommend submitting a revised draft to the peer review portal by next Wednesday so you can get one more round of feedback before the final deadline.
Derek: I'll do that. Thank you for the guidance.
Professor Lin: Of course. And remember, contradictory feedback isn't a problem, it's an opportunity to clarify your thinking.

options: To discuss contradictory peer review feedback on his draft

To ask about changing his topic
questions.explanation: Derek says his two peer reviewers gave him contradictory feedback and he's confused about how to revise, so he's visiting the professor for guidance.

Social media algorithms reinforcing political polarization by prioritizing engaging content
The history of political polarization in the US

options: Citing an established index like the Esteban-Ray polarization measure
Counting the number of political posts
questions.explanation: Professor Lin recommends citing an established index like the Esteban-Ray polarization measure and explaining how it applies to Derek's dataset.
